sites.name: Colorado Ute Power Plant / Durango Light & Power Building
sites.location: 14th Street at the Animas River, Durango
overview: Completed in 1893, this Mission-style power plant helped supply electricity to Durango and the San Juan mining region. History Colorado identifies it as Colorado's earliest known Mission-style building and an unusual industrial use of the style.
timeline: 1889–1893 — Durango expanded its electric system and completed the present steam-power building at 14th Street and the Animas River.
1909 — A transmission line from Tacoma brought hydroelectric service to the Durango plant, while lines were extended toward Silverton and nearby mining areas.
1916–1917 — Major additions installed General Electric turbine-generator equipment and expanded generating capacity.
1946–1949 — Boilers were converted to gas, and the plant received a west-side expansion and new equipment.
1972 — After declining demand, the plant was judged impractical to continue operating.
moreHistory: The National Register nomination ties the plant to the development of Durango and the San Juan mining district. It also documents the building's stepped parapet, bell-tower forms, surviving historic equipment, and rare Mission-style treatment of an industrial facility. The map point identifies the historic building; current interior access and operating conditions should be confirmed locally.

sites.name: Small Hope Mine
sites.location: La Plata Mining District (California Mining District)
overview: Small Hope Mine is a historic gold-silver mine in the La Plata Mining District of La Plata County. Federal geologic work documents a developed mine with a deep shaft, a short adit, and later underground connection attempts from the Grassy Hill crosscut tunnel.
timeline: Late 1880s to early 1890s — The Small Hope vein was discovered and the mine became a recurring producer.
By the late 1890s — Ore was being taken from a 275-foot shaft and a short adit near 11,600 feet elevation; some ore was treated in a small bromination plant.
1898–1900 — The Grassy Hill crosscut tunnel was driven and intersected a vein believed by operators to be the Small Hope, followed by additional drifting.
1930s — Federal investigators recorded the Grassy Hill tunnel as reopened for examination before later caving near its portal.
moreHistory: The retained identification anchor is the La Plata district Small Hope locality at approximately 37.43333, -108.04111. This record intentionally excludes the separate lower-elevation Small Hope feature shown on the Hesperus quadrangle. Historical descriptions document substantial underground development, but this app record does not imply that any shaft, adit, or tunnel is open, safe, or accessible today.
